When the loop moves at the same speed in the three different directions shown in the image, in which case is the induced current in the loop maximum?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a long straight horizontal wire above the rectangular loops, with current I directed to the right along the wire. Below it are three cases of the same rectangular closed loop. In case I, the loop moves horizontally to the right, parallel to the wire. In case II, the loop moves downward, away from the wire. In case III, the loop has a dot-in-circle velocity symbol indicating motion out of the page. Reasoning: The magnetic field produced by the long straight wire is perpendicular to the plane of the loop at the initial position, and its magnitude decreases as the distance from the wire increases. The induced current depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux through the loop. In case I, translating parallel to the wire keeps every part of the loop at the same distance from the wire, so the flux does not change and the induced current is zero. In case III, motion out of the page from the initial plane does not give the largest initial change of flux through the loop, so it is not the maximum case. In case II, the loop moves away from the wire into a weaker magnetic field, so the magnetic flux through the loop changes at a nonzero rate. Therefore the induced current is maximum in case II.

raw_record.question_text: A rectangular closed loop is placed near an infinitely long current-carrying straight wire. Initially, the loop is in the same plane as the wire, with two sides of the loop parallel to the wire. When the loop moves at the same speed in the three different directions shown in the image, in which case is the induced current in the loop maximum?

method.method_draft: First describe the image: identify the wire above the loop, current direction, and the three loop velocities: I parallel to the wire, II away from the wire, III out of the page. Then reason from flux. For points in the loop’s plane below the wire, the magnetic field through the loop is perpendicular to the loop and has magnitude decreasing with distance from the wire. In case I, the loop moves sideways, so every part of the loop remains at the same distance from the wire; the flux is unchanged, so induced current is zero. In case III, the indicated out-of-page motion does not produce a larger change of the flux through the loop at the initial configuration, and is not the maximum case. In case II, the loop moves downward, so the whole loop moves into a region of weaker magnetic field; the flux through the loop changes at a nonzero rate. Therefore the induced current is maximum in case II.

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: Uses the standard Faraday-law magnetic-flux comparison, directly tied to the three visually shown velocity directions; this is the natural single route for the problem.
planner_metadata.image_role: Read the diagram as an infinite horizontal straight wire at the top carrying current to the right. The rectangular loop lies below it. Case I shows the loop translating horizontally to the right, parallel to the wire; case II shows it translating downward, away from the wire; case III shows a circled-dot velocity symbol indicating motion perpendicular to the page.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the text statement that the loop is rectangular, closed, initially coplanar with an infinitely long current-carrying straight wire, and that the speeds in the three shown directions are equal; compare induced current magnitudes across the three cases.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Use the magnetic field of a long straight wire, B = μ0I/(2πr), whose magnitude depends only on distance from the wire. Use Faraday’s law: induced current magnitude is proportional to |dΦ/dt|. A change in magnetic flux through the loop is required for induction; translating parallel to equal-distance contours does not change flux, and motion parallel to the local field/normal direction as shown in III gives no larger flux change initially. Downward motion changes the loop’s distance from the wire and hence changes the flux most.
